# Locality Guide: Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain (1790–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Municipality:** Pozuelo, Province of Albacete, Autonomous Community of Castilla-La Mancha, Spain
- **Coordinates:** 38.8092°N, 2.1014°W
- **FamilySearch place record:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/research/places/?text=Pozuelo&focusedId=9074893
- **Wikipedia:** https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pozuelo_(Albacete)
- **Parent province (modern):** Albacete (created 1833). During 1790–1820, the civil administration was the **Intendencia de La Mancha** within the kingdom of Castilla-La Nueva.
- **Ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** **Diocese of Albacete**. Parish church: **San Bartolomé de Pozuelo**.
- **Population during period:** Population data were not returned by the place_population tool for this municipality. The Catastro de Ensenada (1749–1756) is the nearest census source but predates the target window; Pozuelo was a small rural municipality.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural; cereal crops and livestock typical of the Castilian meseta.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (effectively 100% of population); the Catholic Church was the sole record-keeper for vital events through 1869.
- **Key historical events affecting records:** The Peninsular War (Guerra de la Independencia, 1808–1814) — French occupation of Spain — may have disrupted local administration and, in some parishes, caused record gaps or losses. Researchers should check image continuity for 1808–1814 specifically.

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1833:** Pozuelo fell within the Intendencia de La Mancha (Castilla-La Nueva). No separate Province of Albacete existed.
- **1833:** The Javier de Burgos territorial reform created the modern Province of Albacete. All subsequent civil administration records are provincial.
- **Ecclesiastical boundaries:** The Diocese of Albacete has administered Pozuelo throughout the period of record; the diocesan archive holds the centralized parish registers.
- For 1790–1820, records follow the **Diocese of Albacete** (ecclesiastical) and the **Intendencia de La Mancha** (civil), not modern provincial lines.

## Available record types

### Church records (primary source for 1790–1820)
- **Denomination:** Roman Catholic exclusively.
- **Parish:** San Bartolomé, Pozuelo.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (bautizos), marriages (matrimonios), burials (entierros/defunciones). Confirmations occasionally recorded with baptisms.
- **Language:** Castilian Spanish; earlier entries (pre-c.1800) may contain Latin passages.

- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images + partial index (77–95% by volume). Not full-text searchable.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** 1870 (effective 1871 in most municipalities).
- **Not applicable for 1800–1810.** Civil registration did not exist. Parish records are the sole vital-event source for this period.

### Census / padrón records
- **Catastro de Ensenada, 1749–1756:** [FamilySearch collection 1851392](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1851392) — images only; predates target period but may establish family names and landholdings.
- **No indexed municipal padrón for Albacete covering 1790–1820** is available on FamilySearch or identified via external links.
- The Archivo Histórico Provincial de Albacete may hold manuscript padrones; contact in person or by correspondence.

### Military records
- **Peninsular War (1808–1814):** Service records for this period are held at the Archivo General Militar de Segovia and the Archivo Histórico Nacional (AHN).
- [Spain, Soldier Personal Service Files, 1835-1981](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2558684) — indexed & images on FamilySearch; earliest date 1835, so post-dates 1800–1810 window.
- Officer personal files (1400s–1900s, mostly 1700s–1800s): http://bibliotecavirtualdefensa.es/BVMDefensa/i18n/consulta/registro.cmd?id=4816
- Spain Ministry of Defense: http://www.defensa.gob.es

### Notarial records
- Notarial records for Albacete are referenced in the FamilySearch wiki. Holdings for Pozuelo-area notaries would be at the **Archivo Histórico Provincial de Albacete**. No online collection specifically covering Pozuelo's notarial records for 1790–1820 was found.

## Proof Summary: Infant Son Juan Rodríguez, Buried 17 February 1801, Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain

**Research question:** Do the baptismal and burial records of Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain document a son named Juan, born to Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia, who was baptized and died in infancy circa 1801?

### Introduction

This summary evaluates whether an infant son named Juan, child of the married couple Juan Rodríguez Martínez (born 16 November 1777, Pozuelo, Albacete) and Marcelina Garcia (born 25 April 1779, Pozuelo, Albacete), was born and died in infancy in Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain circa 1801. The question arose from a gap in the known family record: the couple's children documented by baptismal register span 1799 to 1822, but no baptism record for a son named Juan in 1801 had been located.

### Research Scope

To answer this question, the FamilySearch collection "España, Diócesis de Albacete, registros parroquiales, 1504-1979" (collection 1431011) — the primary repository for Catholic parish registers of the Diocese of Albacete covering Pozuelo — was searched via three indexed baptism query variants targeting the name Juan with parents Juan Rodríguez and Marcelina Garcia in Pozuelo circa 1800–1802. No baptism record for this child was found across any variant. A separate indexed burial search was also executed, which returned the record examined below. The original register image was read and transcribed, superseding the index. No other repository is expected to hold contradicting primary evidence for this event.

### The Burial Record

The original parish burial register of San Bartolomé, Pozuelo, Diocese of Albacete, contains the following entry dated 17 February 1801, as transcribed from image ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-691S-222:

> *[Margin label] Parbulo. Juan hijo de Juan Rodriguez y Marcelina Garcia*
>
> *En la Yglesia Parroq.ª del S.º S.º Bartholome Ap. se enterró en Pozuelo en diezisiete dias del mes de Febrero de mil ochocientos y uno, se enterró a Juan parbulo hijo de Juan Rodriguez, y Marcelina Garcia, y en fe de ello lo firmé D.º Fran.co Blan. y Figueroa*

In translation: "In the Parish Church of the Holy Apostle Saint Bartholomew, was buried in Pozuelo on the seventeenth day of the month of February of eighteen hundred and one, Juan párvulo son of Juan Rodriguez and Marcelina Garcia, and in witness thereof I signed, D. Francisco Blan. y Figueroa."

This record names the deceased as **Juan**, a **párvulo** (an infant or young child who had not yet reached the age of reason), son of **Juan Rodriguez** and **Marcelina Garcia**, buried on **17 February 1801** in the parish church of San Bartolomé, Pozuelo.

**Source classification:** The original parish register is an **original source** — it is the first recording of the event, in the hand of the officiating priest D. Francisco Blanco y Figueroa. The information regarding the burial itself (date, place, child's name, parents' names, and párvulo status) is **primary information** — recorded at the time of the event by the officiating official with direct knowledge. The evidence for the specific facts at issue (that a child named Juan, son of Juan Rodriguez and Marcelina Garcia, was buried in infancy) is **direct evidence** — the record explicitly and completely states each of these facts. This is the strongest possible evidentiary classification.

### Identification of the Parents

The father named "Juan Rodriguez" in this burial entry is identified with **confident** probability as Juan Rodríguez Martínez (tree person 9634-PS9), who was born in Pozuelo, Albacete (baptized 19 November 1777 at San Bartolomé) and was resident in Pozuelo throughout this period. In Spanish Catholic practice of this era, a father's compound surname (Rodríguez Martínez) is characteristically abbreviated to the first surname alone in a child's burial entry; the omission of "Martínez" is therefore fully expected and does not diminish identification. The name, parish, and the co-listing of wife "Marcelina Garcia" — who exactly matches tree person Marcelina Garcia (963H-MBM), the known wife of Juan Rodríguez Martínez — together constitute strong corroborating identification of both parents.

### The Absent Baptism Record

No baptism record for a son Juan born to this couple circa 1801 was found across three indexed search variants covering the Diocese of Albacete baptism collection (77–90% indexed for this period). This absence is not a conflict; it is negative evidence **consistent** with early infant death. In the Catholic canonical practice of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Spain, *párvulos* were those who died before reaching the age of reason (approximately seven years), but in practice the designation was most commonly applied to neonates and infants who died within days or weeks of birth — sometimes before emergency baptism could be administered, or with a baptism recorded on a now-missing or unindexed folio. The burial record itself is the expected surviving documentary trace for a child who died in earliest infancy. The unindexed fraction (10–23%) of the baptism collection means a baptism entry cannot be entirely ruled out; if one exists, it would corroborate the burial entry but could not plausibly contradict it.

### Conclusion

The evidence strongly suggests that the parish burial register of San Bartolomé, Pozuelo, Diocese of Albacete, documents an infant son named Juan, child of Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia, who was buried on 17 February 1801, designated as a *párvulo* (died in infancy). The original parish register — an original source with primary, direct information written by the officiating priest contemporaneously with the burial — directly and completely answers the research question for the burial event.

This conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than Proved for one reason: only a single independent source documents this child's existence and death. GPS "Proved" requires two or more independent original sources with primary information in agreement. No baptism record was found to serve as an independent corroborating source. The single burial record is, however, strong and direct; the tier of Probable reflects the single-source limitation, not any weakness in the record itself.

This conclusion rests on the best evidence currently available. Should a baptism record for this child be located in future research — whether from an unindexed image in collection 1431011 or any other repository — reassessment would be warranted and would likely elevate the tier to Proved.
